patient_info:
You are in a GP surgery.
Name: Gemma Phillips
Age: 42 DOB: 19/06/1984
After introductions, in response to the student’s opening question or comment, please say:
"Hello doctor, I’ve been getting these awful severe spasms of pain under my right ribs, and it happened again last night."
(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a 42-year-old primary school teacher and usually fit and well. Over the last three weeks, you have experienced three episodes of severe, crampy pain in the right upper part of your abdomen, just beneath your ribs.

The pain typically comes on about an hour after eating an evening meal, especially after rich or fatty food—the first time was after fish and chips, and last night’s attack was after a takeaway korma curry. The pain builds rapidly to a crescendo over twenty minutes, remains severely intense for roughly two to three hours, and then gradually fades away completely, leaving you feeling washed out and tender. When it peaks, you would rate the pain as an 8 or 9 out of 10. During the attacks, the pain radiates through into your back and up towards your right shoulder blade. Paracetamol and ibuprofen do not seem to touch it; you find that clutching a hot water bottle while lying curled up gives a tiny amount of comfort.

You feel distinctly nauseated during the episodes and vomited once last night, bringing up clear fluid and undigested food. However, you have had no high temperatures, chills, or shivers. You have not noticed any yellow tinge to your skin or the whites of your eyes. Your urine has remained its usual light straw colour and your stools look entirely normal brown (not pale or grey). You do not suffer from heartburn, burning indigestion, or pain when swallowing. Your bowel movements are regular with no blood or black tarry stools, and you have no urinary burning or loin pain.

You have two children (aged 10 and 8), both born via uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. You have no other medical conditions and have never had abdominal surgery. You take the combined oral contraceptive pill (Microgynon 30) and occasional paracetamol. You have no known allergies to medications.

You do not smoke. You drink 1 or 2 small glasses of wine on a Friday or Saturday night (around 4 units a week). Your diet has become a bit reliant on convenience food recently due to busy school terms. Your mother had her gallbladder removed when she was in her late forties due to gallstones.

You are frightened that the pain might indicate a stomach ulcer or something sinister like bowel or stomach cancer because it is so severe. You are hoping the GP can work out what is going on and organise an ultrasound or prescribe something strong to stop the attacks.
After the consultation has progressed a little please ask the following question
“What do you think is causing these attacks, and what tests will I need?”

examiner_info:
Questions
1. Could you briefly summarise your findings, and state your primary diagnosis and differential diagnoses?
Answer: The candidate should summarise a 42-year-old female presenting with episodic right upper quadrant and epigastric pain provoked by fatty meals, radiating to the back/shoulder, accompanied by nausea, without fever or jaundice. The primary diagnosis is symptomatic cholelithiasis (biliary colic). Differential diagnoses include acute cholecystitis, peptic ulcer disease / gastritis, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or acute pancreatitis.
2. What initial investigations would you recommend to confirm the diagnosis and check for complications?
Answer: The candidate should recommend: 1) A transabdominal ultrasound of the upper abdomen/biliary tree (investigation of choice to identify gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, or common bile duct dilatation), and 2) Blood tests including full blood count (FBC), liver function tests (LFTs including bilirubin and ALP), inflammatory markers (CRP), renal function (U&Es), and serum amylase/lipase to exclude complications such as cholecystitis, cholangitis, choledocholithiasis, or pancreatitis.

patient_info:
You are in a GP surgery.
Name: Chloe Davies
Age: 38 DOB: 15/06/1988
After introductions, in response to the student’s opening question or comment, please say:
"My eyes have been feeling really sore and gritty recently, and they look quite strange in the mirror."
(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a 38-year-old primary school teacher. Over the last three to four months, you have noticed persistent discomfort in both eyes. They constantly feel gritty, dry, and irritated, like there is sand trapped under your eyelids. They water a lot in the wind, and bright sunlight has started to bother you so much that you have to wear sunglasses even on cloudy days. Over the past month, your eyelids have looked swollen and puffy, especially first thing in the morning.

About six weeks ago, you started noticing that your eyes look prominent and 'staring' in photographs. A colleague at school even asked if you were feeling startled or surprised. Over the last two weeks, you have developed intermittent double vision, particularly when looking upwards or sideways when writing on the whiteboard. When you look upwards, there is also a dull, deep ache behind your eyeballs. Your vision itself is not completely blacked out, but it can be slightly blurry when the double vision happens. If asked specifically, your ability to see colours normally has not changed, and you have not had any crusting, yellow discharge, or fever.

When asked about your general health over the last few months, you realise you have felt unusually hot and sweaty compared to everyone else, even keeping your classroom windows wide open. You have lost about 4 kg over the past four months despite having a healthy appetite. You have felt jittery, your hands have a fine tremble, and you frequently feel your heart fluttering or racing in your chest. Your periods have become lighter and slightly irregular, and your bowels have been opening twice a day with loose stools rather than your usual once a day. You had put much of this down to the stress of a recent school inspection.

You have no significant past medical history and take no regular prescribed medications. You have tried over-the-counter sterile saline eye drops, which only gave temporary relief for a few minutes. You take occasional paracetamol for headaches. You have no known drug allergies.

You smoke 15 cigarettes a day and have smoked for the last 18 years. You drink around 4 to 6 units of wine on weekends. You live with your partner and have no children. Your mother has an underactive thyroid and takes levothyroxine, and your maternal aunt had surgery on her neck for an overactive thyroid years ago.

You wondered if you might have developed an allergy to the classroom hamster or chalk dust, or maybe chronic conjunctivitis. However, you are increasingly terrified that your eyes are permanently bulging out, which makes you feel self-conscious, and you worry you might lose your sight from the double vision. You hope the doctor can find out what is going on, give you stronger drops, and refer you to an eye specialist.
After the consultation has progressed a little please ask the following question
“What do you think is causing my eye problems, and what tests will I need?”
When a student asks a question not covered in the information provided, please give a vague or non-committal reply such as "I’m not sure about that", or "I can’t really remember".
examiner_info:
Questions
1. What initial investigations would you arrange for this patient?
Answer: Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4, free T3) and TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb). Assessment of visual acuity and colour vision (e.g. Ishihara plates to check for optic nerve compression). Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist or dedicated joint thyroid-eye clinic.
2. Outline your management plan for this patient.
Answer: Strongly advise and support smoking cessation (the most important modifiable risk factor). Provide symptomatic relief (artificial tears/ocular lubricants, sunglasses, head elevation at night). Refer urgently to ophthalmology/specialist thyroid eye disease clinic. Refer to endocrinology for medical management of hyperthyroidism (e.g. antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole). Explain red flag symptoms of sight loss requiring emergency review.

patient_info:
You are in the Acute Medical Unit.
Name: David Campbell
Age: 44 DOB: 21/02/1982
After introductions, in response to the student’s opening question or comment, please say:
"Doctor, my legs have become really weak over the last couple of days, and now I have noticed tingling in my fingers as well."
(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a secondary school history teacher and are usually fit, active, and well. Three days ago, you began noticing a pins and needles sensation in both feet and toes. By the following morning, both your legs felt heavy and weak. Over the last 48 hours, this weakness has climbed rapidly up your legs. You now struggle significantly to stand from a low chair and cannot manage the stairs at home without leaning heavily on the bannister. Yesterday evening, the tingling spread into both of your hands, and your grip feels noticeably weaker when holding a pen or opening a jar.

Approximately two and a half weeks ago, you suffered a severe bout of gastroenteritis with profuse diarrhoea and stomach cramps after eating barbecued chicken. That illness completely resolved after four or five days, and you felt completely back to normal until this weakness began.

You have not had any back pain, neck pain, or injury to your spine. You have had no problems controlling your bladder or bowels, with no incontinence and no difficulty passing urine. You have not noticed any facial droop, visual disturbance, double vision, or trouble speaking, chewing, or swallowing. However, this morning you noticed you felt a little breathless when trying to talk in full sentences or when lying flat. You do not have a fever, headache, or stiff neck. You have never had any episodes of muscle weakness or numbness in the past.

You have a mild history of asthma, which is well controlled; you only use a salbutamol inhaler once or twice a year when you have a cold. You do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter supplements, or illicit substances. You have no known drug or environmental allergies.

There is no family history of neurological conditions, autoimmune disease, or muscle disorders. Your father died in his seventies from ischaemic heart disease.

You live with your wife and two teenage children in a two-storey house. You are a non-smoker and drink approximately 4 to 6 units of alcohol per week (a pint or two of beer on weekends). Prior to this episode, you ran 5 kilometres twice a week.

You are extremely anxious because the weakness seems to be progressing upwards every day. You wonder whether this is related to the recent food poisoning or if you have trapped a nerve in your spine. Your main concern is that the weakness will reach your chest and stop you from breathing properly, or that you might end up permanently paralysed. You expect the doctors to admit you, run tests to find out what is causing this rapid deterioration, and start treatment to stop it spreading further.
After the consultation has progressed a little please ask the following question
“What do you think is the cause, and what tests will I need?”
When a student asks a question not covered in the information provided, please give a vague or non-committal reply such as "I’m not sure about that", or "I can’t really remember".
examiner_info:
Questions
1. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what other differential diagnoses would you consider?
Answer: The most likely diagnosis is Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy), supported by symmetrical ascending motor weakness, distal paraesthesias, and a recent campylobacter-type diarrhoeal illness. Differentials include spinal cord compression, transverse myelitis, cauda equina syndrome, myasthenia gravis, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, and functional neurological disorder.
2. What are your immediate next steps in terms of monitoring, investigation, and management?
Answer: Immediate priority is respiratory monitoring with regular bedside forced vital capacity (FVC) measurements and monitoring for autonomic instability (telemetry/blood pressure). Key investigations include a lumbar puncture (looking for albuminocytological dissociation), nerve conduction studies/EMG, and basic bloods (electrolytes, CK). Definitive management involves admission (often HDU/ITU level) and immunotherapy with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) or plasma exchange, alongside supportive care and VTE prophylaxis.

Name: Nicola Campbell
Age: 42 DOB: 01/04/1984
After introductions, in response to the student’s opening question or comment, please say:
"I've just been feeling really low and exhausted lately, and I'm struggling to get through each day."
(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a primary school teacher and usually active and healthy. Over the past three to four months, you have developed a persistent low mood and profound fatigue that has crept up on you. You find yourself feeling flat and tearful, and you have lost all enthusiasm for activities you normally enjoy, such as gardening and reading with your book club. You feel mentally sluggish and struggle to plan your lessons or stay focused in the classroom. You are sleeping nine to ten hours a night but still wake up feeling completely unrefreshed, although you do not wake up abnormally early in the morning.

After introductions, in response to the student’s opening question or comment, please say:

(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a 58-year-old accountant who is usually in reasonably good health. Earlier today around 2:00 PM, while helping your son move heavy garden furniture, you suddenly felt extremely unwell. You broke out in a cold, drenching sweat and noticed a vigorous tremor in both hands. Your heart felt like it was racing in your chest and you felt ravenously hungry.

Within ten minutes, you became dizzy and lightheaded. Your wife tells you that you became confused, repetitive, and disorientated, asking if you needed to submit tax returns and slurring your words slightly. You have no memory of about fifteen minutes of this period. Your wife immediately recognised something was wrong, sat you down, and gave you a large glass of regular full-sugar cola and two biscuits. Within 15 minutes of drinking the cola, the sweating, shaking, and confusion completely cleared up. Your wife insisted on bringing you to the Emergency Department.

You had skipped lunch today because you were busy in the garden, having only had a small bowl of porridge at 7:00 AM. You have never had an episode like this before and have never had "hypo" symptoms previously. You did not collapse, lose consciousness, bite your tongue, or wet yourself. You had no chest tightness, shortness of breath, headache, facial droop, or weakness in your arms or legs. You have had no fever, cough, burning with urination, or recent illnesses.

You have a history of Type 2 diabetes diagnosed four years ago and high blood pressure. At your routine diabetic review ten days ago, your practice nurse noted your sugar levels were running high and added a new tablet called gliclazide (40 mg once daily with breakfast) to your usual metformin. You also take ramipril 5 mg once daily and atorvastatin 20 mg once daily. You have no allergies.

You do not smoke. You drink 2 to 3 units of alcohol over the weekend, but you have had none today or yesterday. You drive a car to work every day. There is a family history of Type 2 diabetes in your mother, but no history of epilepsy or stroke.

You are worried that you might have suffered a stroke, "mini-stroke" (TIA), or early dementia. You are eager to know what caused this sudden turn and whether your medications need changing.
After the consultation has progressed a little please ask the following question
“What do you think is the cause and what tests will I need?”

Questions

Answer: The primary diagnosis is drug-induced hypoglycaemia (secondary to gliclazide, compounded by missed meal and exertion). Differentials to consider include transient ischaemic attack (TIA), focal or generalised seizure, cardiac arrhythmia, or an acute panic attack.

(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a retired secondary school science teacher and used to be reasonably active. Over the past four months, you have had three distinct chest infections. Each time you developed a productive cough with greenish phlegm, mild feverishness, and wheeze, requiring a course of amoxicillin or doxycycline from the GP. While the antibiotics cleared the acute chestiness, you never felt like you bounced back fully, and the infections keep recurring every few weeks.

Alongside these infections, you have developed deep, nagging lower back pain over the last three months. It is worse when you walk or bend to do light gardening and eases slightly when you lie flat. You initially put it down to wear-and-tear or lifting compost bags, but paracetamol barely touches it. Crucially, you have no pain shooting down your legs, no numbness around your groin or buttocks, no leg weakness, and no problems controlling your bladder or bowels.

Over the same timeframe, you have been profoundly fatigued, feeling washed out even after a full night's sleep. You have noticed you are drinking far more water than usual because your mouth constantly feels dry, and you have become prone to constipation over the past month. You have unintentionally lost about 4 kg over the past twelve weeks. You have not had drenching night sweats, swollen glands in your neck or armpits, unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or blood in your urine or stools.

You have a history of mild hypertension diagnosed eight years ago and bilateral knee osteoarthritis. You take amlodipine 5 mg once daily and occasional paracetamol 1 g for your knees. You have no drug allergies.

You live with your wife in a two-storey house. You are an ex-smoker; you stopped smoking 20 years ago having smoked around 10 cigarettes a day for 15 years. You drink roughly 4 to 6 units of red wine per week. Your father died of colon cancer at age 79 and your mother had a stroke in her eighties; there is no family history of blood or bone marrow cancers.

You are worried that your immune system is failing or that there might be an underlying cancer causing your infections, weight loss, and back ache. You are hoping the doctor will run some blood tests and get to the bottom of why your body cannot fight off these bugs.

Age: 58 DOB: 15/03/1968
After introductions, in response to the student’s opening question or comment, please say:
"Doctor, I've noticed a shaking in my right hand over the last few months and it's starting to worry me."
(Please ensure you use this wording every time, to ensure consistency)
You are a 58-year-old surveyor and have generally been fit and well. You enjoy walking and gardening, though you feel like everyday physical tasks have started taking you longer over the past twelve months.

About eight months ago, you noticed an intermittent trembling in your right hand. It is most obvious when you are resting, such as sitting back in a chair watching the television or sitting in team meetings with your hands on your lap. When you deliberately reach out to pick up a mug or type, the shaking tends to settle down, but your right fingers feel somewhat stiff and clumsy. You have also noticed that your handwriting has become noticeably smaller, cramped, and untidy across the page. For nearly a year, your right shoulder and arm have felt tight and aching; your physiotherapist wondered if it was a frozen shoulder, but the exercises did not relieve it. When walking, your wife pointed out that you keep your right arm still rather than swinging it, and your right foot sometimes scuffs or drags slightly when you are tired.

The tremor does not affect your left hand, your head, or your voice. Having an alcoholic drink does not reduce or stop the tremor. You have had no falls, blackouts, or unsteadiness when standing up. You have no double vision or trouble looking up or down, and you have no difficulty swallowing or choking on food. Your memory, concentration, and thinking are completely normal. You have had no heat intolerance, sweating, or heart palpitations, and your bladder and bowels work without any sudden leakage or difficulty.

Thinking back, you lost most of your sense of smell two or three years ago; you can barely smell petrol or fresh coffee. Your wife has also complained that over the last year you have been restless at night, frequently shouting, thrashing, and kicking your legs during vivid dreams. You have also suffered from dry, infrequent bowel motions (constipation) for the past year, which was never an issue before.

You have high blood pressure, diagnosed five years ago, which is well controlled. You have never had a stroke or serious head injury. You take bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg once daily. You do not take any regular indigestion remedies, anti-sickness tablets (like metoclopramide or prochlorperazine), or psychiatric medications. You have no known allergies.

Neither of your parents nor your two brothers have ever had tremors, Parkinson's disease, or any neurological problems. You have never smoked cigarettes. You drink around 4 to 6 units of alcohol per week (a couple of pints of bitter on weekends). You live with your wife in a two-storey house. You are worried that this shaking might be Parkinson's disease, as a former work colleague had it, and you are anxious about losing manual dexterity and having to give up work as a surveyor. You expect the doctor to explain what is likely going on and refer you for the right tests.

“What do you think is the cause and what tests will I need?”

Questions
1. What are the appropriate next steps in investigating and establishing the diagnosis for this patient?
Answer: The candidate should recognise that Parkinson's disease is primarily a clinical diagnosis and explain that NICE guidelines recommend urgent specialist referral (neurologist or elderly care movement disorder specialist) before initiating anti-parkinsonian pharmacotherapy. If diagnostic uncertainty remains after specialist clinical assessment, a 123I-FP-CIT SPECT (DaTscan) or MRI brain may be considered to differentiate from essential tremor or secondary/atypical parkinsonism.

Answer: Urgent bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs showing obstructive/cholestatic picture, coagulation screen, CA 19-9) and urgent imaging such as an abdominal ultrasound scan or urgent triple-phase / pancreatic-protocol contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen.
